addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

# Todo

This file uses [Prose form](agent-data/prose.md#prose-form). It contains near term tasks with a
short description and uses links or reference links for more details.

## In Progress

A cycle's record has one home at a time, and while the cycle runs this is it. At Preparation
the picked-up `## Todo` item **moves** here (never copied, one home per text) and becomes six
provisional items, all required, all revised as steps land. At close-out the whole block moves
into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` and becomes that cycle's `##` section. It is never written in
two places. Shape:

```
### <type>: <title>

#### Problem
<what is wrong, a sentence or two>

#### Solution
<what will be done about it, broad; provisional until the close-out>

#### Acceptance check
<the measure of "are you finished?">

#### Ladder
- [[N]] [<cycle title> opening][M] (done)
- [[N]] [<title>][M] (current)
- [[N]] [<title>][M]
- [[N]] [<cycle title> closing][M]

#### Deliberation
<how the five above were decided; `_None._` if there was nothing to deliberate>

#### Ladder details
<one `#####` subsection per rung, closing included, headed by its exact title, opened at
laddering with the rung's intent and completed at landing with the conceptual delta, the
closing rung's at close-out with gotchas in problem/solution form>
```

A multi-cycle program adds one level: the program is the `###`, its current cycle the `####`,
and the six items sit one level below that (headings give the current work durable anchors,
which numbered Todo entries can't). Full rules in
[cycle-protocol.md](agent-data/cycle-protocol.md#preparation); the move's four transforms are
in [Chores sections](agent-data/cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).

_No cycle currently in progress._

## Todo

Entries are in **strict priority rank**, #1 highest, descending. Reprioritize by moving an
entry, then `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run TODO.md` to renumber. The numbers are positional rank,
not stable IDs. To refer to a Todo, name it by its **title** (a greppable mention; a numbered
list item has no anchor to link to), not its number. Long-tail entries live in
[todo-backlog.md](notes/todo-backlog.md). Use the
[Prose form](agent-data/prose.md#prose-form); deeper detail goes in
`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` design subsections (link via `[N]` ref).

1. Prepare for expected errors: before a command whose outcome is not clean (a rebase across
   diverged lines, a force-push, dogfooding a dev tool), state the expected output, what

1	# custom-family.md - iiac-perf's layer, as a member of the vc-x1 agent-file family
2	
3	Read after [custom.md](custom.md), whose single convention entry points here. Present only in a
4	member repo: a project that is not a member does not carry this file, and nothing in it applies to
5	one.
6	
7	**A member's `custom.md` differs from the payload by that one line, and everything of its own lives
8	here.** That is the family's convention and it buys a property worth having: `diff custom.md
9	<template>/work/custom.md` is one line for every member, so the file that can never be pinned still
10	converges, and a member's whole customization surface is this file. The medium below is here for
11	that reason rather than because it has anything to do with the family.
12	
13	## Medium and validation
14	
15	The artifact is the `iiac-perf` CLI, a Rust crate (manifest `Cargo.toml`, package name
16	`iiac-perf`), with versioning specifics in [versioning.md](agent-data/versioning.md).
17	
18	**What a version bump promises**: nothing to a dependent, because there are none. `iiac-perf` is
19	a binary crate with no library target and no external consumers, so `X.Y.Z` is a scope signal to
20	readers of the history (see
21	[Advancing X.Y.Z](agent-data/versioning.md#advancing-xyz-scope-decides)) and not a compatibility
22	contract. Revisit with a compat clause if a library crate ever splits out.
23	
24	- **Full validation**
25	  - when: per-commit checklist step 5
26	  - run as separate invocations, each exit status checked:
27	    1. `cargo fmt`
28	    2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
29	    3. `cargo test`
30	    4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
31	    5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
32	- **Fast validation**
33	  - when: ladder checklist step 3
34	  - `cargo test --bins`
35	
36	The commands are the project's. The rule that each invocation's exit status is checked is
37	universal and lives in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#working-practices).
38	
39	## Membership
40	
41	- **member name**: `iiac-perf`
42	- **template repository**: `../vc-x1-template`
43	
44	These two are environment rather than instruction, the same species as `.vc-config.toml`'s
45	`[repos]` paths, and they belong there instead. They cannot move yet: `vc-x1 config --validate`
46	rejects keys it does not know (measured on 0.78.4, 2026-08-07), so a config carrying them would
47	fail its own validator.
48	
49	## Messaging
50	
51	Members leave word for each other in per-member mailboxes at the template repository. The protocol
52	is `../vc-x1-template/MESSAGES.md` and it governs. These are the parts that decide how a session
53	behaves.
54	
55	- **At acquaint, check `../vc-x1-template/messages/iiac-perf.md`.** An absent file means no mail.
56	- **Handle, then delete** the entry, and delete the file once it empties. Mailboxes hold open items
57	  only.
58	- **So a message can never be a record.** Anything in one worth keeping is copied into
59	  `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` *before* the entry is deleted. Learned 2026-08-05, when a
60	  convergence message carried measurements that would have been lost with it.
61	- **Messages are thin pointers, not state.** Durable coordination state lives in topical files,
62	  and a message says "action needed, see <file>" rather than restating the details.
63	- **Write to a member's mailbox, never into their repo.** A repo with a live session is written
64	  only by its own agent.
65	
66	## Dogfood log
67	
68	Dated entries on what this project is trying and where the pinned instructions chafed, failed, or
69	got amended: the evidence base for the family's convergence decisions
70	([Changing the agent-files](AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
71	
72	Each entry carries a **status**: `proposed` (in our agent-files, awaiting the family),
73	`adopted family-wide`, `rejected`, or `permanently local`. In-flight entries only: on
74	resolution an entry retires to [done.md](notes/done.md) with its narrative in
75	`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, adopted and rejected alike. Entries predating the status
76	convention keep their form until touched.
77	
78	- 2026-08-14 (`proposed`): the semicolon allowance goes, and the agent-files sweep to zero
79	  - the pinned rule blessed the "between equals" join and left everything else a judgment call.
80	    wink's observation: agents take advantage of the exceptions, so the allowance is claimed
81	    wherever a semicolon is wanted
82	  - the rule is now flat: prose carries no semicolons, and a semicolon appears only in code
83	    (code spans, fenced code, source files), where it is syntax. Each prose site converts to a
84	    period, a comma with a conjunction, or sub-bullets
85	  - the agent-files (custom* included) carry no historical exemption and sweep to zero. Any
86	    other historical file keeps its semicolons only until altered, and altering one means
87	    asking the user whether they should go (wink, tightened mid-rung from a silent
88	    convert-when-touched). Excluding src/'s ~125 existing comment-line joins from this cycle's
89	    sweep is wink's call, keeping it focused on agent-file convergence
90	  - the rule tightened is one vc-x1 wrote and swept at ~140 sites. Proposed to them by message
91	    after this cycle lands, with their own instruction back: review the rule, not each instance
92	  - rationale in
93	    [chores-07](notes/chores/chores-07.md#docs-semicolons-leave-the-agent-files)
94	
95	- 2026-08-12 (`proposed`): validation runs at every commit, and the notes-only skip goes
96	  - the per-commit checklist stamped the version-of-record at step 4 and let step 5 be skipped
97	    for notes-only commits, so a commit could carry a version that no build ever had. Measured
98	    the same day: 0.24.5 and 0.24.6 both stamped and neither built, and `-V` answered 0.24.4
99	    until the next close-out jumped it three
100	  - wink's rule and his reason: every commit bumps the version precisely so a build exists
101	    carrying it, which makes an unbuilt bump a version nobody can run and the banner a claim
102	    nobody checked
103	  - so the skip goes at all three sites, and the step is conditioned on the medium rather than on
104	    the commit: run the artifact if the medium has one to run (wink). A first draft made the
105	    escape "too costly to build", which asks every project to judge its own cost and would be
106	    claimed by anyone who found validation tedious
107	  - each of the three sites gets one job so the rule is written once (wink): the checklist
108	    instructs, the protocol holds the reason and the medium condition, and `custom.md` holds the
109	    commands. A first pass had the checklist and the protocol carrying the same sentence
110	  - the same pass fixed a step number this morning's sync left stale, and dropped a
111	    cycle-at-a-glance clause that named validation as a close-out specialty. The stale number is
112	    the argument in miniature: it was a restatement, which is what let it drift unnoticed
113	  - rationale in [chores-06](notes/chores/chores-06.md#docs-validate-every-commit)
114	
115	- 2026-08-07 (`proposed`): the family layer splits out of `custom.md`
116	  - `custom.md` had been accumulating things that only make sense because this repo belongs to a
117	    family: a member name, a template path, and a dogfood log whose status vocabulary reads
118	    `adopted family-wide`. wink's test is that `custom.md` should be usable as-is by a project that
119	    has never heard of us, and it failed that test
120	  - so the family layer moves here, and `custom.md` shrinks to a stub with nothing to substitute:
121	    a title naming no project, and one section. A member's copy differs from the payload's by the
122	    single conventions entry that points here, so `diff custom.md <template>/work/custom.md` is one
123	    line for every member
124	  - the pointer is that entry rather than an intro sentence (wink). We argued for the intro, on the
125	    grounds that four members carrying an identical one-line diff looks like a fake divergence.
126	    The answer is that it is a real project convention, and one line is cheaper than a paragraph
127	    every member has to keep in sync
128	  - the chain is `AGENTS.md` -> `custom.md` -> here, all of it prose, which is what lets the pinned
129	    set stay ignorant of the split. A non-member has no entry and no file
130	  - `CLAUDE.md` collapses to one line, `@AGENTS.md` (wink). It had grown a second `@` import per
131	    layer, which made it a second statement of what to read and therefore a second thing to keep
132	    true. Now `AGENTS.md` is the only source of that truth, and `CLAUDE.md` is payload-identical for
133	    every project, member or not. The cost is real and worth stating: nothing below `AGENTS.md` is
134	    auto-loaded any more, so hard rule 0 is load-bearing rather than a formality
135	  - one consequence needs the family's agreement, not ours: **"Check the mailbox at acquaint" leaves
136	    the pinned `AGENTS.md`** and lands in `## Messaging` above. vc-x1 pinned it in the 20260802
137	    snapshot, so this is a reversal. The argument is that a non-member cannot perform it at all,
138	    since building the mailbox path needs a member name and a template path they do not have, so it
139	    is dead text naming concepts they lack rather than a harmless no-op
140	  - deliberately not opened in the same pass: `AGENTS.md` still says "the family" and "member" where
141	    the generic mechanism is "the template payload and my copy of it". Same inconsistency one level
142	    up, and folding it in would roughly double the review surface of an already large configuration
143	
144	- 2026-08-07 (`proposed`): cycles run on a bookmark, and `custom.md` stops holding rules
145	  - the bookmark rule had been adopted in principle since 2026-08-01 and was written down
146	    nowhere: `TODO.md` carried the intention, `cycle.md` said what a topic bookmark *is* once you
147	    have one, and neither creating nor landing one appeared in any agent-file. Two cycles ran on
148	    bookmarks anyway, on undocumented habit
149	  - so hard rule 13 states it, `cycle.md` gains an opening checklist and a land step, and
150	    `jj.md` gains the commands. Landing turns out to be the interesting half: it is the moment
151	    the cycle's commits become permanent, which makes it the trigger for the chores backfill
152	    that waits on permanence. That connection existed and had no owner
153	  - the create and land *commands* are deliberately separable from the rule, because wink
154	    expects a `vc-x1 start-change <bookmark>` to own the create half eventually
155	  - same pass, `custom.md` empties of conventions. Five entries were rules the family already
156	    has or should have, so they moved into the pinned files (two into `prose.md`, one into
157	    `versioning.md`, one into `AGENTS.md`) and two retired as answered
158	  - the sharpened convention behind it (wink): **intent decides the file, and nothing gates the
159	    edit**. A member writes a rule into its local pinned copy whenever it means the family to
160	    take it, without asking. `custom.md` is for what the member does *not* offer the family. The
161	    2026-08-05 entry below framed the same mechanism around experiments, which read as narrower
162	    than it is
163	  - cost, and it is the same one the 2026-08-05 entry recorded: our pinned files now hold more
164	    unreviewed text than before, and nothing at acquaint shows a reader which parts the family
165	    has agreed to. The diff is the answer and reading it is still manual
166	
167	- 2026-08-05 (`proposed`): a step is a title, and the version and the step number both leave the

# custom-family.md - iiac-perf's layer, as a member of the vc-x1 agent-file family

Read after [custom.md](custom.md), whose single convention entry points here. Present only in a
member repo: a project that is not a member does not carry this file, and nothing in it applies to
one.

**A member's `custom.md` differs from the payload by that one line, and everything of its own lives
here.** That is the family's convention and it buys a property worth having: `diff custom.md
<template>/work/custom.md` is one line for every member, so the file that can never be pinned still
converges, and a member's whole customization surface is this file. The medium below is here for
that reason rather than because it has anything to do with the family.

## Medium and validation

The artifact is the `iiac-perf` CLI, a Rust crate (manifest `Cargo.toml`, package name
`iiac-perf`), with versioning specifics in [versioning.md](agent-data/versioning.md).

**What a version bump promises**: nothing to a dependent, because there are none. `iiac-perf` is
a binary crate with no library target and no external consumers, so `X.Y.Z` is a scope signal to
readers of the history (see
[Advancing X.Y.Z](agent-data/versioning.md#advancing-xyz-scope-decides)) and not a compatibility
contract. Revisit with a compat clause if a library crate ever splits out.

- **Full validation**
  - when: per-commit checklist step 5
  - run as separate invocations, each exit status checked:
    1. `cargo fmt`
    2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
    3. `cargo test`
    4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
    5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
- **Fast validation**
  - when: ladder checklist step 3
  - `cargo test --bins`

The commands are the project's. The rule that each invocation's exit status is checked is
universal and lives in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#working-practices).

## Membership

- **member name**: `iiac-perf`
- **template repository**: `../vc-x1-template`

These two are environment rather than instruction, the same species as `.vc-config.toml`'s
`[repos]` paths, and they belong there instead. They cannot move yet: `vc-x1 config --validate`
rejects keys it does not know (measured on 0.78.4, 2026-08-07), so a config carrying them would
fail its own validator.

## Messaging

Members leave word for each other in per-member mailboxes at the template repository. The protocol
is `../vc-x1-template/MESSAGES.md` and it governs. These are the parts that decide how a session
behaves.

- **At acquaint, check `../vc-x1-template/messages/iiac-perf.md`.** An absent file means no mail.
- **Handle, then delete** the entry, and delete the file once it empties. Mailboxes hold open items
  only.
- **So a message can never be a record.** Anything in one worth keeping is copied into
  `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` *before* the entry is deleted. Learned 2026-08-05, when a
  convergence message carried measurements that would have been lost with it.
- **Messages are thin pointers, not state.** Durable coordination state lives in topical files,
  and a message says "action needed, see <file>" rather than restating the details.
- **Write to a member's mailbox, never into their repo.** A repo with a live session is written
  only by its own agent.

## Dogfood log

Dated entries on what this project is trying and where the pinned instructions chafed, failed, or
got amended: the evidence base for the family's convergence decisions
([Changing the agent-files](AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).

Each entry carries a **status**: `proposed` (in our agent-files, awaiting the family),
`adopted family-wide`, `rejected`, or `permanently local`. In-flight entries only: on
resolution an entry retires to [done.md](notes/done.md) with its narrative in
`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, adopted and rejected alike. Entries predating the status
convention keep their form until touched.

- 2026-08-14 (`proposed`): the semicolon allowance goes, and the agent-files sweep to zero
  - the pinned rule blessed the "between equals" join and left everything else a judgment call.
    wink's observation: agents take advantage of the exceptions, so the allowance is claimed
    wherever a semicolon is wanted
  - the rule is now flat: prose carries no semicolons, and a semicolon appears only in code
    (code spans, fenced code, source files), where it is syntax. Each prose site converts to a
    period, a comma with a conjunction, or sub-bullets
  - the agent-files (custom* included) carry no historical exemption and sweep to zero. Any
    other historical file keeps its semicolons only until altered, and altering one means
    asking the user whether they should go (wink, tightened mid-rung from a silent
    convert-when-touched). Excluding src/'s ~125 existing comment-line joins from this cycle's
    sweep is wink's call, keeping it focused on agent-file convergence
  - the rule tightened is one vc-x1 wrote and swept at ~140 sites. Proposed to them by message
    after this cycle lands, with their own instruction back: review the rule, not each instance
  - rationale in

# iiac-perf

Notifications for iiac-perf. The protocol is in [README.md](README.md). The persistence policy
below is this file's own, set by its owner.

New records go directly below this header, newest first.

**Persistence:** records are never deleted. A handled record keeps its place and gains a `read`
timestamp, so this file is the whole inbound history and a sender can see that their message
arrived. Where it led is recorded in the same record's `outcome-local` / `outcome-remote`,
usually a section of iiac-perf's `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`.

content.content:
1	# vc-x1-messages v0.1.0
2	
3	Notifications for the vc-x1 family. Message bodies live in the sender's own repo, this repo holds
4	only pointers to them, one record per message.
5	
6	The version above is the record format's, and changes to it are additive. A field is added, never
7	renamed or repurposed, so a reader written against an older version still reads today's records.
8	A major bump would mean that stopped being true and there has not been one.
9	
10	To send a message create a file with the message and a markdown section header somewhere in your
11	repo. Then add a record to the file named for the destination you find here, directly below that
12	file's own header, so the newest record is first. Whether a push sits between those two steps is
13	[the choice of mode](#two-modes-fast-and-durable) below. A record is a `##` heading and a list of
14	fields and each field is generally "owned" by the creator, although fixing errors is
15	permissible. Every field is optional and records routinely carry only two or three, though a
16	writer aims for at least one of `local` or `remote`, since a record with neither points at
17	nothing.
18	
19	## 2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z iiac-perf
20	
21	- local: [../iiac-perf/messages/test-msg.md#message1](../iiac-perf/messages/test-msg.md#message1)
22	- remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/55554b452957/messages/test-msg.md#message1
23	
24	The heading is `<utc-timestamp> <sender>`. It is also the record's anchor, so a reply or a
25	record elsewhere can link at this exact entry without anyone inventing an id.
26	
27	Then a dash list of `- field: <value>`, where every reference may carry an optional markdown
28	section slug.
29	
30	- `local:` the message's local file reference.
31	- `remote:` the message's remote file reference.
32	- `read:` added by the recipient, a UTC timestamp of when they read it. A record without it is
33	  unread. Receipt is not completion: a record stays open until it carries an outcome, so a
34	  member's open traffic is the records in their file with no `outcome-*` field, and `read` is
35	  what tells the sender their message arrived.
36	- `outcome-local:` / `outcome-remote:` optional, added by the recipient, pointing at what came of
37	  the message, the reply or the record of what was decided. They are what let one record hold
38	  both halves of an exchange, and their arrival is what closes a record.
39	
40	A handled record, this one sent the other way, as it would sit in `iiac-perf.md`. Two things are
41	worth noticing. The body is vc-x1's specimen under `notes/messages/` where iiac-perf's sits
42	under `messages/`, because a body lives wherever its sender chooses. And the `remote:` was
43	written only after the body's commit pushed, the ordering rule from
44	[Two modes](#two-modes-fast-and-durable) obeyed in this very example, since a permalink cannot
45	precede the commit it names. The exchange is staged but every reference is live:
46	
47	## 2026-08-13T20:41:33.512Z vc-x1
48	
49	- local: [[1]]
50	- remote: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/blob/437a1e6b93d2/notes/messages/test-msg.md#message1
51	- read: 2026-08-13T22:04:07.000Z
52	- outcome-local: [[2]]
53	- outcome-remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/55554b452957/notes/chores/chores-07.md#docs-design-the-vc-x1-messages-repo
54	
55	[1]: ../vc-x1/notes/messages/test-msg.md#message1
56	[2]: ../iiac-perf/notes/chores/chores-07.md#docs-design-the-vc-x1-messages-repo
57	
58	**Fields may be added later without breaking what is already written**, which is why a record is
59	a list of named fields rather than a positional line. A reader ignores fields it does not know,
60	and a record missing an optional field is complete as it stands. Prose may sit beside the fields
61	in a record, only the field lines are read. A record carries no version of its own, since its
62	commit dates it against this file's history.
63	
64	**A malformed record is not an error, only less useful**, and a reader takes what is there rather
65	than rejecting it. A heading that lost its sender is even recoverable, since whoever wrote a
66	record committed it. The one part that must be present is the `##` heading itself, because it is
67	what separates one record from the next. Field lines with no heading above them are read as part
68	of the record before, so an interrupted write damages its neighbour rather than itself.
69	
70	## Two modes, fast and durable
71	
72	The message file lives in your repo either way. What differs is whether the record carries a
73	permalink, and that decides both the order of the steps and how long the record stays good for.
74	
75	- **Fast, local only.** Write the message file, add the record with `local` alone, done. No push
76	  and no waiting, and the reader resolves it from their sibling clone.
77	- **Durable.** Write the message file, commit and push it, then add the record with the `remote`
78	  that push made resolvable.
79	
80	**The order matters only in the durable mode, and it is the step people miss.** A permalink names
81	a commit, so it cannot be written before that commit exists and is pushed. Write the record first
82	and you have a URL that 404s until the file catches up with it.
83	
84	**Write a record once, when you have what goes in it.** Writing it early with an empty `remote`
85	costs two writes to this repo for one message, and a reader may follow the empty one, find
86	nothing, and mark it read.
87	
88	Which mode to use is the tradeoff in
89	[The remote reference is a commit permalink](#the-remote-reference-is-a-commit-permalink) below.
90	Same-day traffic between siblings is fine on local alone. Anything worth citing later wants the
91	push.
92	
93	## Whoever writes a record commits it
94	
95	Whoever writes a record is the one who commits it. In the same act is the ideal, since then no
96	moment holds an uncommitted record, but with today's handful of friendly participants a short
97	delay or batching a few writes into one commit is fine. What does not relax is the ownership:
98	nobody commits someone else's writing, which is what this repo has instead of a manager, because
99	ownership is per write rather than per repo.
100	
101	## Concurrent writes collide, and the collision is normal
102	
103	Every new record goes directly below its file's header, so two writers active at the same time
104	conflict at exactly the same lines. The merge is trivial, keep both records in either order, and
105	it is the expected cost of newest-first rather than an error. No record depends on its
106	neighbours, which is what makes the resolution safe.
107	
108	## The remote reference is a commit permalink
109	
110	The remote form is `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<commit-sha>/<path>#<slug>`, and the
111	`<commit-sha>` is not optional.
112	
113	- **A branch name rots.** A topic bookmark is deleted once its cycle lands, and the permanent
114	  branch does not carry the file until then, so both forms break at exactly the moment the
115	  message is worth reading.
116	- **A commit SHA does not.** It survives the bookmark's deletion, survives a rebase of anything
117	  after it, and resolves for a reader with no clone. GitHub's `y` key converts a branch URL into
118	  this form.
119	- **The local form names a path, the remote form names a version.** A local reference resolves to
120	  whatever that file says now, in whatever state that working copy happens to be, and it assumes
121	  the member repos are siblings of this one. A remote reference resolves to what was actually
122	  sent. Local-only is fine for traffic read the same day, anything meant to be read later wants
123	  the remote one.
124	
125	## Each file's owner sets its persistence
126	
127	A member's file belongs to whoever receives on it. They create it, they curate it, and they
128	declare at its head what becomes of a handled record. A sender needs to know none of that, only
129	where to add one.
130	
131	- **Marking beats deleting, and the reason is the sender.** Whether a message was read is
132	  recorded nowhere else, not in the sender's repo and not in the reader's, so a policy that marks
133	  a handled record tells the sender it arrived while one that deletes it tells them nothing.
134	  A recommendation, not a rule.
135	- **Nothing worth keeping is ever only here.** The body is a committed file in the sender's repo,
136	  and that commit carries the `ochid:` trailer linking the session that wrote it. A notification
137	  record can be lost without losing anything, which is what makes owner-chosen policies safe.
138	- **A file that does not exist yet is created by whoever writes first**, carrying no policy until
139	  its owner declares one. Reserving creation to the owner would make the first message to a new
140	  member impossible, since only the owner may create and only the sender wants to. Settled as a
141	  rule at vc-x1's review (2026-08-13): the one real risk, a sender imposing a policy, is already
142	  defused by the no-policy-at-birth clause.
143	
144	## No protection
145	
146	Any member can modify or delete any file here. This is a cooperative store with no access
147	control, so it works only among friendly participants and history is the only recourse.

# vc-x1-messages v0.1.0

Notifications for the vc-x1 family. Message bodies live in the sender's own repo, this repo holds
only pointers to them, one record per message.

The version above is the record format's, and changes to it are additive. A field is added, never
renamed or repurposed, so a reader written against an older version still reads today's records.
A major bump would mean that stopped being true and there has not been one.

To send a message create a file with the message and a markdown section header somewhere in your
repo. Then add a record to the file named for the destination you find here, directly below that
file's own header, so the newest record is first. Whether a push sits between those two steps is
[the choice of mode](#two-modes-fast-and-durable) below. A record is a `##` heading and a list of
fields and each field is generally "owned" by the creator, although fixing errors is
permissible. Every field is optional and records routinely carry only two or three, though a
writer aims for at least one of `local` or `remote`, since a record with neither points at
nothing.

## 2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z iiac-perf

- local: [../iiac-perf/messages/test-msg.md#message1](../iiac-perf/messages/test-msg.md#message1)
- remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/55554b452957/messages/test-msg.md#message1

The heading is `<utc-timestamp> <sender>`. It is also the record's anchor, so a reply or a
record elsewhere can link at this exact entry without anyone inventing an id.

Then a dash list of `- field: <value>`, where every reference may carry an optional markdown
section slug.

- `local:` the message's local file reference.
- `remote:` the message's remote file reference.
- `read:` added by the recipient, a UTC timestamp of when they read it. A record without it is
  unread. Receipt is not completion: a record stays open until it carries an outcome, so a
  member's open traffic is the records in their file with no `outcome-*` field, and `read` is
  what tells the sender their message arrived.
- `outcome-local:` / `outcome-remote:` optional, added by the recipient, pointing at what came of
  the message, the reply or the record of what was decided. They are what let one record hold
  both halves of an exchange, and their arrival is what closes a record.

A handled record, this one sent the other way, as it would sit in `iiac-perf.md`. Two things are
worth noticing. The body is vc-x1's specimen under `notes/messages/` where iiac-perf's sits
under `messages/`, because a body lives wherever its sender chooses. And the `remote:` was
written only after the body's commit pushed, the ordering rule from
[Two modes](#two-modes-fast-and-durable) obeyed in this very example, since a permalink cannot
precede the commit it names. The exchange is staged but every reference is live:

## 2026-08-13T20:41:33.512Z vc-x1

- local: [[1]]
- remote: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/blob/437a1e6b93d2/notes/messages/test-msg.md#message1
- read: 2026-08-13T22:04:07.000Z
- outcome-local: [[2]]
- outcome-remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/55554b452957/notes/chores/chores-07.md#docs-design-the-vc-x1-messages-repo

[1]: ../vc-x1/notes/messages/test-msg.md#message1
[2]: ../iiac-perf/notes/chores/chores-07.md#docs-design-the-vc-x1-messages-repo

**Fields may be added later without breaking what is already written**, which is why a record is
a list of named fields rather than a positional line. A reader ignores fields it does not know,
and a record missing an optional field is complete as it stands. Prose may sit beside the fields
in a record, only the field lines are read. A record carries no version of its own, since its
commit dates it against this file's history.

**A malformed record is not an error, only less useful**, and a reader takes what is there rather
than rejecting it. A heading that lost its sender is even recoverable, since whoever wrote a
record committed it. The one part that must be present is the `##` heading itself, because it is
what separates one record from the next. Field lines with no heading above them are read as part
of the record before, so an interrupted write damages its neighbour rather than itself.

## Two modes, fast and durable

The message file lives in your repo either way. What differs is whether the record carries a
permalink, and that decides both the order of the steps and how long the record stays good for.

- **Fast, local only.** Write the message file, add the record with `local` alone, done. No push
  and no waiting, and the reader resolves it from their sibling clone.
- **Durable.** Write the message file, commit and push it, then add the record with the `remote`
  that push made resolvable.

**The order matters only in the durable mode, and it is the step people miss.** A permalink names
a commit, so it cannot be written before that commit exists and is pushed. Write the record first
and you have a URL that 404s until the file catches up with it.

**Write a record once, when you have what goes in it.** Writing it early with an empty `remote`
costs two writes to this repo for one message, and a reader may follow the empty one, find
nothing, and mark it read.

Which mode to use is the tradeoff in
[The remote reference is a commit permalink](#the-remote-reference-is-a-commit-permalink) below.
Same-day traffic between siblings is fine on local alone. Anything worth citing later wants the
push.

## Whoever writes a record commits it

Whoever writes a record is the one who commits it. In the same act is the ideal, since then no
moment holds an uncommitted record, but with today's handful of friendly participants a short
delay or batching a few writes into one commit is fine. What does not relax is the ownership:
nobody commits someone else's writing, which is what this repo has instead of a manager, because
ownership is per write rather than per repo.

## Concurrent writes collide, and the collision is normal

Every new record goes directly below its file's header, so two writers active at the same time
conflict at exactly the same lines. The merge is trivial, keep both records in either order, and
it is the expected cost of newest-first rather than an error. No record depends on its
neighbours, which is what makes the resolution safe.

## The remote reference is a commit permalink

The remote form is `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<commit-sha>/<path>#<slug>`, and the
`<commit-sha>` is not optional.

- **A branch name rots.** A topic bookmark is deleted once its cycle lands, and the permanent
  branch does not carry the file until then, so both forms break at exactly the moment the
  message is worth reading.
- **A commit SHA does not.** It survives the bookmark's deletion, survives a rebase of anything
  after it, and resolves for a reader with no clone. GitHub's `y` key converts a branch URL into
  this form.
- **The local form names a path, the remote form names a version.** A local reference resolves to
  whatever that file says now, in whatever state that working copy happens to be, and it assumes
  the member repos are siblings of this one. A remote reference resolves to what was actually
  sent. Local-only is fine for traffic read the same day, anything meant to be read later wants
  the remote one.

## Each file's owner sets its persistence

A member's file belongs to whoever receives on it. They create it, they curate it, and they
declare at its head what becomes of a handled record. A sender needs to know none of that, only
where to add one.

- **Marking beats deleting, and the reason is the sender.** Whether a message was read is
  recorded nowhere else, not in the sender's repo and not in the reader's, so a policy that marks
  a handled record tells the sender it arrived while one that deletes it tells them nothing.
  A recommendation, not a rule.
- **Nothing worth keeping is ever only here.** The body is a committed file in the sender's repo,
  and that commit carries the `ochid:` trailer linking the session that wrote it. A notification
  record can be lost without losing anything, which is what makes owner-chosen policies safe.
- **A file that does not exist yet is created by whoever writes first**, carrying no policy until
  its owner declares one. Reserving creation to the owner would make the first message to a new
  member impossible, since only the owner may create and only the sender wants to. Settled as a
  rule at vc-x1's review (2026-08-13): the one real risk, a sender imposing a policy, is already
  defused by the no-policy-at-birth clause.

## No protection

Any member can modify or delete any file here. This is a cooperative store with no access
control, so it works only among friendly participants and history is the only recourse.

1	# Prose and durable text
2	
3	How long-lived text is written on this project: the prose shape, the punctuation rules, and the
4	commit-title identity. Read this before writing durable text (notes files, commit messages, doc
5	comments, chores sections).
6	
7	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
8	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
9	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	## Prose form
12	
13	Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why*
14	or the high-level *what*, sharpened to a *problem statement* where a surface calls for one (see
15	[Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape)), then a `-` bullet list for the details. The width
16	numbers and the wrap discipline live in [Line widths](#line-widths) below, their one home. One
17	fact per bullet or sub-bullet beats a paragraph packing several. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs:
18	they hide the structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without
19	naming their relationship is the same failure at sentence scale. See
20	[Semicolons](#semicolons) and
21	[Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).
22	
23	Surfaces that use this shape:
24	
25	- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files. See
26	  [Doc comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
27	- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and bot-repo). The title is the commit-specific
28	  add-on. See [Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
29	- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`. See
30	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
31	- Todo entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure one-liners
32	  are still fine. Done entries take the same shape with the title bolded, detail always as
33	  sub-bullets rather than sentences trailing off the title line. See
34	  [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form).
35	
36	Bullet *content* differs by surface:
37	
38	- **Commit bodies**: the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) for finished work, arranged
39	  by [Commit-body form](#commit-body-form) below. What is specific to a commit:
40	  - the problem statement defines any word the title assumes, since the title is what a reader
41	    meets first and it answers the problem
42	  - **no file list.** The diff and `git show --stat` are the mechanical record, so restating them
43	    is a second copy that can drift from the first. An import of a thousand files is one change
44	  - these are claims a reader has to follow, so they are sentences rather than fragments. A
45	    bullet wanting a paragraph belongs in the chores section instead
46	  - the **deliberation** stays out: alternatives weighed, evidence, dates, costs accepted. Those
47	    live in the chores section, the `## Todo` entry, and the session the `ochid:` trailer names,
48	    each reachable from the commit by construction. The problem itself is a *why* and belongs
49	    here
50	- **Chores / todo / done**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what
51	  landed and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit
52	  list. See
53	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
54	- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).
55	
56	### Line widths
57	
58	Every width number lives here and nowhere else: the other files and sections link here rather
59	than restating one, so a change is a single edit and the copies cannot drift. Consolidated
60	2026-08-09, when the body width moved and the restatements had to be hunted.
61	
62	- **Prose**, all durable text: wrap at <=100 cols, bullet continuations indented two spaces.
63	- **Source**, doc comments and inline comments included: <=100 cols, which is rustfmt's default
64	  `max_width` (enforcement notes in [code.md](code.md#line-width)).
65	- **Commit titles**: <=50 chars.
66	- **Commit bodies**: <=75 cols, the Linux kernel patch standard. It replaced git's older 72
67	  convention here 2026-08-09, and published bodies keep the wrap they shipped with.
68	
69	The widths are wrap defaults, not absolutes (the title cap excepted). Existing text re-wraps
70	when touched, no mass sweeps. Write to the full width: wrap near the limit rather than
71	imitating the narrow wrap of older text, and a line that reads better long stays long (an URL,
72	a literal report row, indented code in a comment).
73	
74	### Problem-first shape
75	
76	`## In Progress` cycle blocks, chores sections, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper
77	form of the same shape: a problem, then how it is answered, then the steps that get there.
78	
79	- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate
80	  what follows it.
81	- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms,
82	  answering whatever question the problem statement raises. Surface-specific rules are in
83	  [Bullet content differs by surface](#prose-form) above.
84	- **Plan bullets** (the what/when), the steps. Formality differs by surface:
85	  - In Progress / chores: a committed ladder, one step per commit. See
86	    [Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
87	    per-step title + `(current)` / `(done)` form.
88	  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering, formalized only when the entry is
89	    picked up into a cycle.
90	
91	**Timing decides whether the solution statement is provisional, not whether it is written.** A
92	cycle writes one at Preparation, before the work, and revises it as steps land. The close-out's
93	commit body carries the final one. A `## Todo` entry's is provisional in the same way. Only a
94	commit body's is settled, because a commit is finished by the time it has one. The earlier rule
95	here said a plan was for work not yet done and a solution for work that is, which left a cycle
96	unable to say at its opening what it intended to do.
97	
98	### Commit-body form
99	
100	A commit body is the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
101	problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
102	bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a
103	solution statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and
104	separately.
105	
106	- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It
107	  is mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is
108	  a body a `--body` flag can mistake for an option.
109	- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general
110	  problem, not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is
111	  usually asking to be more than one commit.
112	- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and a `-` solves the nearest enclosing problem: nested under a
113	  `*` facet it solves that facet, at top level it solves the intro's general problem, which is
114	  how one solution says it retires every facet at once. Position expresses scope.
115	- **Zero facets is the trivial commit**: a problem paragraph and one or more top-level `-`
116	  solutions. Not a second form, the general form with an empty middle.
117	
118	**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution.
119	Indentation alone cannot separate them in the trivial case, where a lone top-level `-` reads as a
120	solution only because `-` always is one. The typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds
121	every facet, `^- ` and `^  - ` every solution). Bodies are read as plain text, in `jj log` and in
122	terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever flattens them the indentation still
123	carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and a linter's consistent-marker rule
124	is wrong to normalize them.
125	
126	Unchanged by this: no version in title or body, no file list, no deliberation, titles per
127	[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit).
128	
129	### Semicolons
130	
131	Prose carries no semicolons. A semicolon appears only in code (code spans, fenced code, source
132	files), where it is syntax rather than prose. The structure a semicolon would have joined is
133	written explicitly instead:
134	
135	- **Two claims** take a period, each half standing as its own sentence ("The diff empties. The
136	  history keeps the record.").
137	- **A continuation** takes a comma with a conjunction, when one half carries the other's thought
138	  onward rather than making its own claim.
139	- **A list hiding in prose** (`A; B; C` inside a sentence or bullet) breaks into sub-bullets so
140	  the structure shows. List items that themselves contain commas restructure the same way rather
141	  than separating with semicolons.
142	
143	The code allowance is why a bare byte scan cannot enforce the rule: a checker blanks the code
144	first, then expects zero.
145	
146	The agent-files (`AGENTS.md`, `custom*`, `agent-data/*`) carry no historical exemption and are
147	swept to zero. Any other historical file keeps its existing semicolons only until it is altered:
148	altering one is the moment to ask the user whether its semicolons should be removed, always,
149	never a license to convert or keep them silently.
150	
151	### Typeable punctuation only
152	
153	Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal. The prohibition is on
154	*authoring*, not presence: a file may legitimately hold a banned character it transcribed (see
155	below), so a byte scan is not the rule and a sweep needs the authored/transcribed judgment.
156	Banned from authoring: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. None can be entered without a compose key or a
157	paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em dash next to option syntax reads as another flag.
158	Like the semicolon rule above this one is absolute, and stricter with history: no ask-on-alter,
159	no exemption at all, because a banned character costs nothing to write and is paid on every
160	read, so a soft rule accumulates them.
161	
162	`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no single replacement, because an em
163	dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:
164	
165	- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading and a paragraph. Make the body
166	  sub-bullets.
167	- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag) takes a colon, which keeps a
168	  glossary or a command list at one line per entry.
169	- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two sentences. Often the aside should just
170	  go.
171	
172	Converting a heading moves its anchor. The em dash strips but the spaces on both sides survive,
173	so `## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while its colon form slugs to `#a-b` (see
174	[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point inbound links in the same
175	commit.
176	
177	Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker), plus commit titles and
178	everything under `src/`: doc comments, inline comments, and any user-visible string. Source is
179	the surface a human edits and greps most, so an untypeable character costs more there than in
180	prose. It applies going forward, and existing text converts when touched. A code span is not exempt
181	by itself. Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this section names them.
182	A banned character doing a job is a use and converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes
183	`` `.expect(...)` ``.
184	
185	Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an error message, an already-published
186	commit title) is transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether or not it sits
187	in a code span. It matters most for commit titles: converting one stops it matching
188	`git log --grep` and breaks the verbatim identity that
189	[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) requires between
190	a commit title, its chores header, and its `## Done` entry.
191	
192	### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)
193	
194	A ladder step, its chores section, and its commit description share a *title* shape, a
195	[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`,
196	an optional `(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail.
197	They differ in the title's marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies take the
198	[Commit-body form](#commit-body-form), ladder / chores are conceptual (see "Bullet *content*
199	differs by surface" above). The shared template:
200	
201	```
202	<title>                          # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
203	<optional prose intro>
204	  - <optional item>
205	    <optional prose intro>
206	      - <optional sub-item>
207	      ...
208	```
209	
210	The three surfaces apply it as:
211	
212	- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the rung is
213	  `- [[N]] [<title>][M] (marker)`: the as-built `[[N]]` placeholder carried from birth, the
214	  title reference-linked to the rung's subsection via `[M]: #<slug>` in the file's
215	  `# References` (the closing rung linked like the rest), and the `(current)` / `(done)` marker.
216	  Its position in the list is its position in the ladder. The last rung is the close-out and its
217	  text says so. Detail lives not on the rung but in the block's `Ladder details` subsection
218	  headed by the rung's exact title (see the protocol's
219	  [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation)), bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
220	- **Chores section** (`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`): no prefix, since the `##` header *is* the
221	  bare title. The as-built ladder is the first content under it (see
222	  [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
223	- **Commit description**: no prefix. The title is the first line, and the body is the prose
224	  (see [Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description)).
225	
226	The title is **identical** across all three for a given step, so a step's ladder entry, its
227	chores `##` header, and its commit title line up verbatim. A `Ladder details` subsection
228	heading carries the same title, a fourth surface on every rung (the closing rung's exists only
229	when close-out gotchas occurred: see the protocol's
230	[Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation)). Pick the commit title first and reuse it.
231	
232	That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct
233	descriptive title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The cycle's chores
234	section header carries the *cycle title*, the bare name no multi-step commit carries (see the
235	bookends below). To keep a cycle's commits collectable with one `git log --grep`, give the
236	step titles a common greppable stem (e.g. `config loader`).
237	
238	**Cycle bookend titles**: a multi-step cycle's bookend commits are the cycle title plus a
239	suffix, " opening" and " closing", same type (`feat: dynamic warmup opening` /
240	`feat: dynamic warmup closing`), so one `git log --grep "<cycle title>"` returns the pair that
241	brackets the ladder. The bare cycle title is the cycle's *name*: the chores `##` header and
242	the `## Done` entry carry it, and no multi-step commit does, which is also what keeps the
243	closing rung's subsection anchor clear of the section header's. A single-step cycle's one
244	commit is the cycle and keeps the bare title. The type repeats across the pair even though the
245	bookends are mostly bookkeeping: identical prefixes make them scannable. Rungs between keep
246	their own titles on the stem.
247	
248	### Steps are named, not numbered
249	
250	A step has a title and no number. Nothing in a ladder rung, a chores as-built rung, a `## Done`
251	entry, or a commit gives a step an ordinal: a rung's place in the list already *is* its place in
252	the ladder, so a number beside it would restate the position and then have to be maintained.
253	
254	- **The title is the identifier.** A record points at a step by its title, a plain greppable
255	  mention, which is why the title is verbatim-identical across the three surfaces.
256	- **Unambiguous, not globally unique.** Two titles must be distinguishable in the two places a
257	  title is resolved: within its own cycle, so a ladder rung names one step, and within its chores
258	  file, since a `##` header is also an anchor and a repeated slug silently dedupes to the first
259	  one. Across the repo's history a title may repeat.
260	- **Nothing renumbers.** Inserting, reordering or dropping a step edits the ladder list and
261	  nothing else. On an unlanded topic bookmark the rungs that already committed an older ladder
262	  come along. See
263	  [Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts).
264	- **`## Todo` ranks are the exception that stays numbered**, because a priority list has an order
265	  worth reading off (see [Todo format](notes.md#todo-format)). Those numbers are positional too,
266	  and are equally never used as references.
267	
268	### Versions live in the version-of-record only
269	
270	No version appears in durable prose: not in an in-flight ladder rung, a chores header, a commit
271	title, or a commit body. The manifest is the version's only written home (see
272	[versioning.md](versioning.md)), and a commit's version is read from that file at that
273	commit.
274	
275	**Why:** the version is a build stamp answering "which commit produced this artifact", not a name
276	for a step. Written into prose it becomes a second identifier that history is free to invalidate:
277	one renumber of published versions turns every prose mention, transcript and pasted report into
278	residue that needs a decoder to read. A renumber cannot touch a title.
279	
280	**Two surfaces record a version rather than name a step.** Both record a *commit*, never a step,
281	which is what keeps them outside the rule rather than exceptions to it:
282	
283	- **A chores as-built rung** records a version alongside that commit's SHA once the commit is on
284	  a permanent branch. The pair decodes an old `-V` banner or a pasted report. It obeys the SHA's
285	  timing exactly, so a rung on an unlanded branch carries neither (see
286	  [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
287	- **A `## Done` entry**, in `TODO.md` and in `done.md`, carries the close-out's version ahead of
288	  its title (see [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form)). Here the version is the search
289	  key: the question a reader arrives with is "what shipped in 0.42.0", and with no version
290	  written anywhere in the Done list that question has no answer.
291	
292	The two differ in timing, and the reason is the SHA rather than the version. The rung waits
293	because a commit cannot record its own SHA. A Done entry has no SHA to wait for and its version
294	is already in the manifest of the commit it is written in, so it is written at close-out. On an
295	unlanded bookmark it is a draft like the rest of the line
296	([Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts)), and a renumber of
297	published versions rewrites it in the same sweep as the rungs.
298	
299	**How to apply:** name the step by its title and the phase in words ("the close-out", "the
300	opening"). Writing *about* versioning is unaffected: a version named as a specimen, whether in the
301	scheme's own notation, a decoder table, or a narrative about a renumber, is a use of the word
302	rather than an identifier for a step, the same distinction
303	[Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only) draws between naming a character and using
304	one. Existing versioned prose is grandfathered and converts when touched, no sweep.
305	
306	## Pinned files name no project
307	
308	A pinned agent-file states rules and mechanisms. It never names a member project, a member's
309	history, or a member's versions. The vc-x1 *CLI* and its versions are tool facts every member
310	shares and stay. What is barred is a member repo appearing in universal text.
311	
312	**Why:** pinned text is copied to every member, so a project narration reads as the reader's own
313	history ("This project adopted the convention on <date>" arrives in repos that adopted it on a
314	different date or never). And the citation goes stale the moment the named project retires its
315	records, while the rule outlives it.
316	
317	**How to apply:** state the rule and its mechanism in the pinned file, and leave the evidence trail
318	in the records of the project that earned it (chores, dogfood log), reachable from the commit
319	that changed the pinned file. Dates are fine, since a date names a moment, not a member. A
320	specimen in
321	the scheme's own notation (an example version, an example bookmark name) is a use, not a
322	reference, per the same distinction
323	[Versions live in the version-of-record only](#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)
324	draws.
325	
326	## Speculation marker
327	
328	Durable text the bot writes (agent-files, `notes/`, commit bodies, chores sections)
329	should stick to observations and direct descriptions of the code or data. If a mechanism,
330	hypothesis, or causal claim enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a
331	reader can tell the measured from the inferred.
332	
333	**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader (or the bot on a later
334	session) can pick it up as a known fact when it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction
335	worth keeping visible in the written record.
336	
337	**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no marker. Prefix with
338	"We think ..." (or a close variant like "Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism
339	("X wins because Y caches better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal state"), a
340	prediction ("this should scale linearly"), or any reasoning not directly supported by the data
341	on hand.
342	
343	## Plain synopsis after technical explanations
344	
345	When a conversational reply centers on a technical explanation (measurement theory, statistics,
346	hardware behavior), end it with a short plain-language synopsis, no jargon and no symbols, so
347	the reader can check their understanding against the technical version.
348	
349	**Why:** the technical form is precise but easy to misread, and the plain form catches
350	misunderstandings early, when they are cheap.
351	
352	**How to apply:** conversation only, not notes files (a notes entry should already lead with
353	the why). Mark it clearly (e.g. "The plain version:"). A reply that is already plain needs no
354	synopsis.
